name: kill
description: Sends a signal to a process by PID. Despite the name, it can send any signal, not only termination.

flags.description: Send SIGTERM (15): request a graceful shutdown.
-KILL: force-terminate immediately; the process cannot intercept it.
List all signal names and numbers.

examples.explanation: Asks PID 2140 to terminate gracefully, letting it save state and close files.
Force-kills PID 2140. Use only after a normal kill fails — data in memory is lost.
Lists available signals. Ctrl+C in a terminal actually sends SIGINT (2).

about: kill is a shell builtin (and /bin/kill exists too). Signals are the kernel's inter-process notification mechanism — the same mechanism that Ctrl+C (SIGINT) and kill -9 (SIGKILL) use. Only the process owner or root may signal a process.
mistakes: Killing PID 1 — the kernel ignores/protects it, but attempting it signals a misunderstanding of the process tree.
Using -9 before trying a normal kill.
warnings: kill -9 leaves lock files and temp data behind because the process cannot clean up; always escalate gradually (TERM, then KILL).
